name: Money Laundering Networks
title: Money Laundering Networks
answer: Money laundering networks are the webs of accounts, shell companies, intermediaries and counterparties used to move the proceeds of crime so their origin is obscured. In fraud detection and forensics the term covers both the criminal structure itself and the analytical problem of finding it inside transaction data. The work sits at the meeting point of anti money laundering compliance, financial crime investigation and network analysis, and it draws on bank records, corporate registries, payment logs and, increasingly, leaked or purchased data sets.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Money laundering networks are the webs of accounts, shell companies, intermediaries and counterparties used to move the proceeds of crime so their origin is obscured. In fraud detection and forensics the term covers both the criminal structure itself and the analytical problem of finding it inside transaction data. The work sits at the meeting point of anti money laundering compliance, financial crime investigation and network analysis, and it draws on bank records, corporate registries, payment logs and, increasingly, leaked or purchased data sets.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Detection runs on transaction and payment data held by banks, payment processors and fintechs, joined to corporate registry filings, sanctions and politically exposed person lists, and adverse media. Graph databases and entity resolution tooling are common because the object of interest is a relationship, not a single record. Case management systems hold the resulting alerts and investigations, and regulators and financial intelligence units receive the formal reports that come out of them.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts start from an alert or a referral, then resolve entities so that the same person or company is not counted twice under different names. They build a graph of accounts, directors, addresses and transfers, and look for structures that make little commercial sense, such as circular payments, rapid pass through accounts and companies sharing a single registered address. Rules and statistical models flag candidates, and graph based methods help rank clusters for human review. Findings are written up as a suspicious activity report or an investigation file, and the reasoning has to be traceable because it may be tested later.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Anti money laundering obligations are set by national law and by standards issued through the Financial Action Task Force, and they are enforced by supervisors and by criminal prosecution. Banks must identify customers, monitor activity and report suspicion, and failures carry fines and, in some cases, personal liability for officers. Data protection rules constrain how personal data can be shared across borders, which is a persistent friction in cross border cases. Provenance matters in two directions: investigators must be able to show where each piece of evidence came from, and the models used to prioritise alerts must be documented well enough to be defended.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward shared infrastructure, with more jurisdictions building central registries of beneficial ownership and more cross border information exchange between financial intelligence units. Graph learning and large scale entity resolution are being applied to the same problem, which raises the question of how a model's output is explained to a court or a supervisor. Criminals adapt quickly to each control, moving to new payment channels and to crypto assets, so the practical pressure is less on finding a single definitive method and more on shortening the time between detection and a usable case file.
